claim: Olfactory associative learning in Drosophila is mediated by synaptic plasticity between the Kenyon cells of the mushroom body and their output neurons.
source: Olfactory associative learning in Drosophila is mediated by synaptic plasticity between the Kenyon cells of the mushroom body and their output neurons.
evidence: This is a statement in the abstract that represents established knowledge in the field, as evidenced by the extensive citations in the introduction.

claim: Both Kenyon cells and their inputs from projection neurons are cholinergic.
source: Both Kenyon cells and their inputs from projection neurons are cholinergic, yet little is known about the physiological function of muscarinic acetylcholine receptors in learning in adult flies.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations in the main text (Barnstedt et al., 2016; Yasuyama and Salvaterra, 1999).

claim: Aversive olfactory learning in adult flies requires type A muscarinic acetylcholine receptors (mAChR-A), particularly in the gamma subtype of Kenyon cells.
source: Here, we show that aversive olfactory learning in adult flies requires type A muscarinic acetylcholine receptors (mAChR-A), particularly in the gamma subtype of Kenyon cells.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by behavioral experiments shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: mAChR-A inhibits odor responses in Kenyon cells.
source: mAChR-A inhibits odor responses and is localized in Kenyon cell dendrites.
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data in Figures 3-6 showing increased odor responses with mAChR-A knockdown and decreased responses with muscarine application.

claim: mAChR-A is localized in Kenyon cell dendrites.
source: mAChR-A inhibits odor responses and is localized in Kenyon cell dendrites.
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data in Figure 7 showing FLAG-tagged mAChR-A expression in the calyx.

claim: mAChR-A knockdown impairs the learning-associated depression of odor responses in a mushroom body output neuron.
source: Moreover, mAChR-A knockdown impairs the learning-associated depression of odor responses in a mushroom body output neuron.
evidence: This is supported by imaging data in Figure 8 showing that mAChR-A knockdown prevents training-induced depression of MB-MVP2 responses.

claim: mAChR-A function in Kenyon cell dendrites is required for synaptic plasticity between Kenyon cells and their output neurons.
source: Our results suggest that mAChR-A function in Kenyon cell dendrites is required for synaptic plasticity between Kenyon cells and their output neurons.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the combination of localization data (Figure 7) and plasticity data (Figure 8).

claim: Drosophila larvae with reduced mAChR-A expression in KCs show impaired aversive olfactory learning.
source: Drosophila larvae with reduced mAChR-A expression in KCs show impaired aversive olfactory learning (Silva et al., 2015), but it remains unknown whether mAChR-A in KCs also functions in learning in adult flies.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Silva et al., 2015.

claim: Both UAS-RNAi lines (RNAi 1 and RNAi 2) strongly reduce mAChR-A levels when expressed pan-neuronally.
source: Both RNAi lines strongly reduce mAChR-A levels (RNAi 1: 39 ± 8% of elav-GAL4 control, or 61 ± 8% below normal; RNAi 2: 43 ± 10% of normal; mean ± s.e.m.; see Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Knocking down mAChR-A in KCs using OK107-GAL4 significantly reduces short-term aversive learning in adult flies.
source: Under these conditions, both UAS-RNAi transgenes significantly reduced aversive learning, whether training against MCH or OCT (Figure 1B,C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1B,C.

claim: Knocking down mAChR-A did not affect learning when flies were trained with a more intense shock (90 V instead of 50 V).
source: Interestingly, knocking down mAChR-A did not affect learning when we trained flies with a more intense shock (90 V instead of 50 V, Figure 1—figure supplement 1), suggesting that mAChR-A may only be required for learning with moderate intensity reinforcement, not severe reinforcement.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: mAChR-A may only be required for learning with moderate intensity reinforcement, not severe reinforcement.
source: Interestingly, knocking down mAChR-A did not affect learning when we trained flies with a more intense shock (90 V instead of 50 V, Figure 1—figure supplement 1), suggesting that mAChR-A may only be required for learning with moderate intensity reinforcement, not severe reinforcement.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the differential effects of mAChR-A knockdown at different shock intensities.

claim: Knocking down mAChR-A had no effect on naïve avoidance of MCH and OCT.
source: Consistent with this, knocking down mAChR-A had no effect on naïve avoidance of MCH and OCT (Figure 1D; see Materials and methods) or flies' reaction to electric shock (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), showing that the defect was specific to learning, rather than reflecting a failure to detect odors or shock.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Knocking down mAChR-A had no effect on flies' reaction to electric shock.
source: Consistent with this, knocking down mAChR-A had no effect on naïve avoidance of MCH and OCT (Figure 1D; see Materials and methods) or flies' reaction to electric shock (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), showing that the defect was specific to learning, rather than reflecting a failure to detect odors or shock.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Adult-only knockdown of mAChR-A in KCs reduced learning.
source: Flies were grown at 23°C until 3 days after eclosion and were then transferred to 31°C for 7 days. Adult-only knockdown of mAChR-A in KCs reduced learning (Figure 1E), just as constitutive knockdown did, indicating that mAChR-A plays a physiological, not purely developmental, role in aversive learning.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data using GAL80ts shown in Figure 1E.

claim: mAChR-A plays a physiological, not purely developmental, role in aversive learning.
source: Adult-only knockdown of mAChR-A in KCs reduced learning (Figure 1E), just as constitutive knockdown did, indicating that mAChR-A plays a physiological, not purely developmental, role in aversive learning.
evidence: This is an inference from the adult-only knockdown experiment shown in Figure 1E.

claim: mAChR-A-MiMIC-GAL4 drove GFP expression in the αβ and γ lobes, but not the α′β′ lobes of the mushroom body.
source: mAChR-A-MiMIC-GAL4 drove GFP expression throughout the brain, consistent with previous reports (Blake et al., 1993; Croset et al., 2018; Davie et al., 2018; Hannan and Hall, 1996) and with the fact that the Drosophila brain is mostly cholinergic. In the mushroom bodies, GFP was expressed in the αβ and γ lobes, but not the α′β′ lobes (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: mAChR-A is more highly expressed in αβ and γ KCs than in α′β′ KCs according to single-cell transcriptomic analysis.
source: Consistent with these MiMIC results, two recently reported databases of single-cell transcriptomic analysis of the Drosophila brain (Croset et al., 2018; Davie et al., 2018) confirm that mAChR-A is more highly expressed in αβ and γ KCs than in α′β′ KCs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by single-cell transcriptome data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and citations to Croset et al., 2018 and Davie et al., 2018.

claim: Learning scores were reduced when mAChR-A RNAi 1 was expressed in αβ and γ KCs or γ KCs alone, but not when expressed in αβ or α′β′ KCs.
source: Learning scores were reduced compared to controls when mAChR-A RNAi 1 was expressed in αβ and γ KCs or γ KCs alone, but not when mAChR-A RNAi 1 was expressed in αβ or α′β′ KCs. (mean ± SEM, n (left to right): 69, 41, 70, 76, 69, 66, 71, 50, 68, **p<0.01, ***p<0.001, Kruskal-Wallis test with Dunn's multiple comparisons test).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: mAChR-A is specifically required in γ KCs for aversive olfactory learning and short-term memory.
source: These results suggest that mAChR-A is specifically required in γ KCs for aversive olfactory learning and short-term memory.
evidence: This is an inference from the KC subtype-specific knockdown experiments shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Knocking down mAChR-A in KCs increased odor-evoked Ca2+ influx in the mushroom body calyx.
source: Knocking down mAChR-A in KCs increased odor-evoked Ca2+ influx in the mushroom body calyx, where KC dendrites reside (Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 3.

claim: mAChR-A is a Gq-coupled receptor whose activation leads to Ca2+ release from internal stores.
source: This result is somewhat surprising because mAChR-A is a Gq-coupled receptor whose activation leads to Ca2+ release from internal stores (Ren et al., 2015), which predicts that mAChR-A knockdown should decrease, not increase, odor-evoked Ca2+ influx in KCs.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ren et al., 2015.

claim: Only in the γ lobe was the effect of mAChR-A knockdown on odor responses statistically significant for both MCH and OCT.
source: Indeed, although odor responses in all lobes were increased by mAChR-A knockdown, only in the γ lobe was the effect statistically significant for both MCH and OCT (Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 3.

claim: mAChR-A knockdown did not affect the sparseness or inter-odor correlation of KC population odor responses when GCaMP6f and mAChR-A-RNAi 2 were expressed in all KCs.
source: When GCaMP6f and mAChR-A-RNAi 2 were expressed in all KCs, mAChR-A knockdown did not affect the sparseness or inter-odor correlation of KC population odor responses (Figure 4A–C) even though it increased overall calyx responses.
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 4A-C.

claim: γ-only expression of mAChR-A-RNAi 1 increased odor responses in the calyx and, in the case of OCT, in the γ lobe.
source: GCaMP6f was visible mainly in the γ lobe (Figure 4D). γ-only expression of mAChR-A-RNAi 1 increased odor responses in the calyx (here, dendrites of γ KCs only) and, in the case of OCT, in the γ lobe (Figure 4E,F).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 4E,F.

claim: γ-only expression of mAChR-A-RNAi 1 did not affect the sparseness or inter-odor correlation of γ KCs.
source: As with pan-KC expression, γ-only expression of mAChR-A-RNAi 1 did not affect the sparseness or inter-odor correlation of γ KCs (Figure 4G–I).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 4G-I.

claim: mAChR-A knockdown does not impair learning through increased overlap in KC population odor representations.
source: Thus, mAChR-A knockdown does not impair learning through increased overlap in KC population odor representations.
evidence: This is an inference from the sparseness and correlation data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Muscarine strongly decreased odor responses in all subtypes of KCs.
source: Muscarine strongly decreased odor responses in all subtypes of KCs (Figure 5A,B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 5A,B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Muscarine did not significantly affect the amplitude of odor responses in PN axons in the calyx.
source: However, muscarine did not significantly affect the amplitude of odor responses in PN axons in the calyx (Figure 5C), suggesting that the effect of muscarine on KCs arose in KCs, not earlier in the olfactory pathway.
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The effect of muscarine on KCs arose in KCs, not earlier in the olfactory pathway.
source: However, muscarine did not significantly affect the amplitude of odor responses in PN axons in the calyx (Figure 5C), suggesting that the effect of muscarine on KCs arose in KCs, not earlier in the olfactory pathway.
evidence: This is an inference from the PN imaging data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Muscarine decreased KC odor responses both in control hemispheres and hemispheres where APL synaptic output was blocked by tetanus toxin.
source: Muscarine decreased KC odor responses both in control hemispheres and hemispheres where APL synaptic output was blocked by tetanus toxin (Figure 5D), and the effect of muscarine was not significantly different between the two cases (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 5D,E.

claim: Muscarine does not act solely by activating APL or by enhancing inhibition on KCs.
source: This result indicates that muscarine does not act solely by activating APL or by enhancing inhibition on KCs (e.g. increasing membrane localization of GABAA receptors).
evidence: This is an inference from the APL-TNT experiment shown in Figure 5D,E.

claim: Applying muscarine to the calyx in the absence of odor stimuli increased GCaMP6f signal in the calyx and α lobe.
source: Surprisingly, applying muscarine to the calyx in the absence of odor stimuli increased GCaMP6f signal in the calyx and α lobe, with small increases in the β and γ lobe that were not statistically significant (Figure 6A,C).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 6A,C.

claim: Applying muscarine to the calyx decreased GCaMP6f signal in the α′ and β′ lobes around 1–2 s after application.
source: It also decreased GCaMP6f signal in the α′ and β′ lobes around 1–2 s after application (Figure 6A), although this effect was also not statistically significant.
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Applying muscarine to the calyx did not increase the calyx odor response.
source: The increased Ca2+ in the calyx most likely did not reflect increased excitability, as applying muscarine to the calyx did not increase the calyx odor response (Figure 6D,E).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 6D,E.

claim: Applying muscarine to the calyx suppressed odor responses in KC axons.
source: Indeed, applying muscarine to the calyx suppressed odor responses in KC axons (Figure 6D,E).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 6D,E.

claim: Overexpressed FLAG-tagged mAChR-A in KCs was only observed in the calyx.
source: When we overexpressed FLAG-tagged mAChR-A in KCs using OK107-GAL4, we only observed anti-FLAG staining in the calyx (Figure 7A), suggesting that mAChR-A is localized to the calyx.
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: mAChR-A is localized to the calyx.
source: When we overexpressed FLAG-tagged mAChR-A in KCs using OK107-GAL4, we only observed anti-FLAG staining in the calyx (Figure 7A), suggesting that mAChR-A is localized to the calyx.
evidence: This is an inference from the immunostaining data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The MiMIC-stop allele is a strongly hypomorphic allele with almost total lack of mAChR-A mRNA.
source: The original MiMIC allele with a GFP insertion in the 5' UTR intron of mAChR-A contains a stop cassette and polyadenylation signal, and indeed, it is a strongly hypomorphic allele: qPCR shows almost total lack of mAChR-A mRNA in the 'MiMIC-stop' allele (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Flies homozygous for the 'MiMIC-stop' allele are viable but show impaired learning.
source: Flies homozygous for the 'MiMIC-stop' allele are viable but show impaired learning, while learning is significantly improved by using mb247-GAL4 to overexpress mAChR-A-FLAG in αβ and γ KCs (Figure 7C), indicating that overexpressed mAChR-A-FLAG can support learning.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Overexpressed mAChR-A-FLAG can support learning.
source: Flies homozygous for the 'MiMIC-stop' allele are viable but show impaired learning, while learning is significantly improved by using mb247-GAL4 to overexpress mAChR-A-FLAG in αβ and γ KCs (Figure 7C), indicating that overexpressed mAChR-A-FLAG can support learning.
evidence: This is an inference from the rescue experiment shown in Figure 7C.

claim: mAChR-A exerts its effect on learning in KC dendrites.
source: These results suggest that mAChR-A exerts its effect on learning in KC dendrites, consistent with the effect of locally applying muscarine to KC dendrites.
evidence: This is an inference from the localization and rescue data shown in Figure 7.

claim: Aversive conditioning reduces MB-MVP2's responses to the aversively-trained odor.
source: For example, aversive memory requires an output neuron downstream of γ KCs, called MBON-γ1pedc>α/β or MB-MVP2. MB-MVP2 leads to approach behavior (Aso et al., 2014b), and aversive conditioning reduces MB-MVP2's responses to the aversively-trained odor (Hige et al., 2015; Perisse et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Aso et al., 2014b; Hige et al., 2015; Perisse et al., 2016.

claim: In control flies not expressing mAChR-A RNAi, the MCH/OCT ratio was substantially reduced in trained flies relative to mock-trained flies.
source: Consistent with previous published results (Hige et al., 2015; Perisse et al., 2016), in control flies not expressing mAChR-A RNAi, the MCH/OCT ratio was substantially reduced in trained flies relative to mock-trained flies (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 8B and citations to Hige et al., 2015; Perisse et al., 2016.

claim: In flies expressing mAChR-A RNAi in KCs, the MCH/OCT ratio was the same between trained and mock-trained flies.
source: In contrast, in flies expressing mAChR-A RNAi in KCs, the MCH/OCT ratio was the same between trained and mock-trained flies (Figure 8B), indicating that the mAChR-A knockdown impaired the learning-related depression of the KC to MB-MVP2 synapse.
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: mAChR-A knockdown impaired the learning-related depression of the KC to MB-MVP2 synapse.
source: In contrast, in flies expressing mAChR-A RNAi in KCs, the MCH/OCT ratio was the same between trained and mock-trained flies (Figure 8B), indicating that the mAChR-A knockdown impaired the learning-related depression of the KC to MB-MVP2 synapse.
evidence: This is an inference from the imaging data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: mAChR-A function in KC dendrites is necessary for learning-related synaptic plasticity in KC axons.
source: This result suggests that mAChR-A function in KC dendrites is necessary for learning-related synaptic plasticity in KC axons.
evidence: This is an inference from the MB-MVP2 imaging data shown in Figure 8.

claim: mAChR-A is required in KCs for aversive olfactory learning in adult Drosophila.
source: Here, we show that mAChR-A is required in KCs for aversive olfactory learning in adult Drosophila.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by behavioral experiments shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Genetic and pharmacological manipulations of mAChR-A suggest that mAChR-A is inhibitory and acts on KC dendrites.
source: Surprisingly, genetic and pharmacological manipulations of mAChR-A suggest that mAChR-A is inhibitory and acts on KC dendrites.
evidence: This is an inference from the combined genetic (Figures 3-4) and pharmacological (Figures 5-6) data, along with localization data (Figure 7).

claim: Dendritically acting mAChR-A is required for synaptic depression between KCs and their outputs.
source: We suggest that dendritically acting mAChR-A is required for synaptic depression between KCs and their outputs.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the combined findings from localization and plasticity experiments.

claim: Drosophila mAChR-A seems to use 'M1-type' signaling via Gq protein when heterologously expressed in CHO cells.
source: Drosophila mAChR-A seems to use 'M1-type' signaling: when heterologously expressed in Chinese hamster ovary (CHO) cells, it signals via Gq protein (Collin et al., 2013; Ren et al., 2015) to activate phospholipase C, which produces inositol trisphosphate to release Ca2+ from internal stores.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Collin et al., 2013 and Ren et al., 2015.

claim: mAChR-A is required for aversive olfactory learning in Drosophila larvae.
source: Recent work indicates that mAChR-A is required for aversive olfactory learning in Drosophila larvae, as knocking down mAChR-A expression in KCs impairs learning (Silva et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Silva et al., 2015.

claim: In adult flies Gq signaling downstream of the dopamine receptor Damb promotes forgetting, not learning.
source: However, it is unclear whether mAChR-A is involved in olfactory learning in adult Drosophila, given that mAChR-A is thought to signal through Gq, and in adult flies Gq signaling downstream of the dopamine receptor Damb promotes forgetting, not learning (Berry et al., 2012; Himmelreich et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Berry et al., 2012 and Himmelreich et al., 2017.

claim: Flies can learn to associate an odor (conditioned stimulus, CS) with a positive (sugar) or a negative (electric shock) unconditioned stimulus (US).
source: Flies can learn to associate an odor (conditioned stimulus, CS) with a positive (sugar) or a negative (electric shock) unconditioned stimulus (US), so that they later approach 'rewarded' odors and avoid 'punished' odors.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of Drosophila learning and memory.

claim: The association between odor and reinforcement is thought to be formed in the presynaptic terminals of the ~2000 Kenyon cells (KCs) that make up the mushroom body (MB).
source: This association is thought to be formed in the presynaptic terminals of the ~2000 Kenyon cells (KCs) that make up the mushroom body (MB), the fly's olfactory memory center (Busto et al., 2010; Cognigni et al., 2018; Hige, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Busto et al., 2010; Cognigni et al., 2018; Hige, 2018.

claim: KCs are activated by odors via second-order olfactory neurons called projection neurons (PNs).
source: These KCs are activated by odors via second-order olfactory neurons called projection neurons (PNs).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: Each odor elicits responses in a sparse subset of KCs.
source: Each odor elicits responses in a sparse subset of KCs (Campbell et al., 2013; Lin et al., 2014) so that odor identity is encoded in which KCs respond to each odor.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Campbell et al., 2013 and Lin et al., 2014.

claim: When an odor (CS) is paired with reward/punishment (US), an odor-specific set of KCs is activated at the same time that dopaminergic neurons (DANs) release dopamine onto KC presynaptic terminals.
source: When an odor (CS) is paired with reward/punishment (US), an odor-specific set of KCs is activated at the same time that dopaminergic neurons (DANs) release dopamine onto KC presynaptic terminals.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: The coincident activation causes long-term depression (LTD) of synapses from the odor-activated KCs onto mushroom body output neurons (MBONs) that lead to approach or avoidance behavior.
source: The coincident activation causes long-term depression (LTD) of synapses from the odor-activated KCs onto mushroom body output neurons (MBONs) that lead to approach or avoidance behavior (Aso and Rubin, 2016; Aso et al., 2014b; Cohn et al., 2015; Hige et al., 2015; Owald et al., 2015; Perisse et al., 2016; Séjourné et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Aso and Rubin, 2016; Aso et al., 2014b; Cohn et al., 2015; Hige et al., 2015; Owald et al., 2015; Perisse et al., 2016; Séjourné et al., 2011.

claim: Training specifically depresses KC-MBON synapses of the 'wrong' valence.
source: In particular, training specifically depresses KC-MBON synapses of the 'wrong' valence (e.g. odor-punishment pairing depresses odor responses of MBONs that lead to approach behavior), because different pairs of 'matching' DANs/MBONs (e.g. punishment/approach, reward/avoidance) innervate distinct regions along KC axons (Aso et al., 2014a).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Aso et al., 2014a.

claim: KCs express both ionotropic (nicotinic) and metabotropic (muscarinic) acetylcholine receptors.
source: Both MB input (PNs) and output (KCs) are cholinergic (Barnstedt et al., 2016; Yasuyama and Salvaterra, 1999), and KCs express both ionotropic (nicotinic) and metabotropic (muscarinic) acetylcholine receptors (Crocker et al., 2016; Croset et al., 2018; Davie et al., 2018; Shih et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Crocker et al., 2016; Croset et al., 2018; Davie et al., 2018; Shih et al., 2019.

claim: The nicotinic receptors mediate fast excitatory synaptic currents.
source: The nicotinic receptors mediate fast excitatory synaptic currents (Su and O'Dowd, 2003), while the physiological function of the muscarinic receptors is unknown.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Su and O'Dowd, 2003.

claim: mAChR-A is the most closely homologous to mammalian mAChRs out of the three mAChRs in Drosophila.
source: Muscarinic acetylcholine receptors (mAChRs) are G-protein-coupled receptors; out of the three mAChRs in Drosophila (mAChR-A, mAChR-B and mAChR-C), mAChR-A (also called Dm1, mAcR-60C or mAChR) is the most closely homologous to mammalian mAChRs (Collin et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Collin et al., 2013.

claim: Mammalian mAChRs are typically divided between 'M1-type' (M1/M3/M5), which signal via Gq and are generally excitatory, and 'M2-type' (M2/M4), which signal via Gi/o and are generally inhibitory.
source: Mammalian mAChRs are typically divided between 'M1-type' (M1/M3/M5), which signal via Gq and are generally excitatory, and 'M2-type' (M2/M4), which signal via Gi/o and are generally inhibitory (Caulfield and Birdsall, 1998).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Caulfield and Birdsall, 1998.

claim: Drosophila mAChR-B is 1000-fold less sensitive to muscarine than mAChR-A is.
source: Initially, we bath-applied 10 µM muscarine, an mAChR-A agonist (Drosophila mAChR-B is 1000-fold less sensitive to muscarine than mAChR-A is [Collin et al., 2013], and mAChR-C is not expressed in the brain [Davie et al., 2018]).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Collin et al., 2013.

claim: mAChR-C is not expressed in the brain.
source: Initially, we bath-applied 10 µM muscarine, an mAChR-A agonist (Drosophila mAChR-B is 1000-fold less sensitive to muscarine than mAChR-A is [Collin et al., 2013], and mAChR-C is not expressed in the brain [Davie et al., 2018]).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Davie et al., 2018.

claim: KCs can be silenced by an inhibitory GABAergic neuron called the anterior paired lateral (APL) neuron.
source: KCs can be silenced by an inhibitory GABAergic neuron called the anterior paired lateral (APL) neuron (Lin et al., 2014; Masuda-Nakagawa et al., 2014; Papadopoulou et al., 2011), so we asked whether muscarine reduces KC odor responses indirectly by activating APL, rather than directly inhibiting KCs.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lin et al., 2014; Masuda-Nakagawa et al., 2014; Papadopoulou et al., 2011.

claim: M1/M3/M5 receptors acting via Gq can inhibit voltage-dependent Ca2+ channels.
source: However, Gq signaling may exert different effects on different neurons in the fly brain, and some examples exist of inhibitory Gq signaling by mammalian mAChRs. M1/M3/M5 receptors acting via Gq can inhibit voltage-dependent Ca2+ channels (Gamper et al., 2004; Kammermeier et al., 2000; Keum et al., 2014; Suh et al., 2010), reduce voltage-gated Na +currents (Cantrell et al., 1996), or trigger surface transport of KCNQ channels (Jiang et al., 2015), thus increasing inhibitory K+ currents.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gamper et al., 2004; Kammermeier et al., 2000; Keum et al., 2014; Suh et al., 2010.

claim: M1/M3/M5 receptors acting via Gq can reduce voltage-gated Na+ currents.
source: However, Gq signaling may exert different effects on different neurons in the fly brain, and some examples exist of inhibitory Gq signaling by mammalian mAChRs. M1/M3/M5 receptors acting via Gq can inhibit voltage-dependent Ca2+ channels (Gamper et al., 2004; Kammermeier et al., 2000; Keum et al., 2014; Suh et al., 2010), reduce voltage-gated Na +currents (Cantrell et al., 1996), or trigger surface transport of KCNQ channels (Jiang et al., 2015), thus increasing inhibitory K+ currents.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Cantrell et al., 1996.

claim: M1/M3/M5 receptors acting via Gq can trigger surface transport of KCNQ channels, thus increasing inhibitory K+ currents.
source: However, Gq signaling may exert different effects on different neurons in the fly brain, and some examples exist of inhibitory Gq signaling by mammalian mAChRs. M1/M3/M5 receptors acting via Gq can inhibit voltage-dependent Ca2+ channels (Gamper et al., 2004; Kammermeier et al., 2000; Keum et al., 2014; Suh et al., 2010), reduce voltage-gated Na +currents (Cantrell et al., 1996), or trigger surface transport of KCNQ channels (Jiang et al., 2015), thus increasing inhibitory K+ currents.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Jiang et al., 2015.

claim: KCs themselves are cholinergic and release neurotransmitter in both the calyx and lobes.
source: However, KCs themselves are cholinergic (Barnstedt et al., 2016) and release neurotransmitter in both the calyx and lobes (Christiansen et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Barnstedt et al., 2016 and Christiansen et al., 2011.

claim: KCs form synapses on each other in the calyx.
source: KCs form synapses on each other in the calyx (Zheng et al., 2018), possibly allowing mAChR-A to mediate lateral inhibition, in conjunction with the lateral inhibition provided by the GABAergic APL neuron (Lin et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Zheng et al., 2018.

claim: mAChR-A may mediate lateral inhibition in conjunction with the lateral inhibition provided by the GABAergic APL neuron.
source: KCs form synapses on each other in the calyx (Zheng et al., 2018), possibly allowing mAChR-A to mediate lateral inhibition, in conjunction with the lateral inhibition provided by the GABAergic APL neuron (Lin et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a speculation based on the known properties of KC-KC synapses and APL function.

claim: Knocking down GABA synthesis in the inhibitory APL neuron increases odor-evoked Ca2+ influx in KCs.
source: For example, knocking down GABA synthesis in the inhibitory APL neuron increases odor-evoked Ca2+ influx in KCs (Lei et al., 2013; Lin et al., 2014) and improves olfactory learning (Liu and Davis, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lei et al., 2013 and Lin et al., 2014.

claim: Knocking down GABA synthesis in the inhibitory APL neuron improves olfactory learning.
source: For example, knocking down GABA synthesis in the inhibitory APL neuron increases odor-evoked Ca2+ influx in KCs (Lei et al., 2013; Lin et al., 2014) and improves olfactory learning (Liu and Davis, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Liu and Davis, 2009.

claim: Rutabaga is generally believed to be the coincidence detector in KC axons that detects when odor coincides with dopamine.
source: Such changes in the action potential waveform may not be detected by calcium imaging, but could potentially affect a 'coincidence detector' in KC axons that detects when odor (i.e. KC activity) coincides with reward/punishment (i.e. dopamine). This coincidence detector is generally believed to be the Ca2+-dependent adenylyl cyclase rutabaga (Levin et al., 1992).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Levin et al., 1992.

claim: Rutabaga mutations do not abolish learning (mutants have ~40–50% of normal learning scores).
source: In addition, rutabaga mutations do not abolish learning (mutants have ~40–50% of normal learning scores) (Yildizoglu et al., 2015), so there may be additional coincidence detection mechanisms affected by action potential waveforms.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Yildizoglu et al., 2015.

claim: Both mAChR-A and the dopamine receptor Damb signal through Gq.
source: Another intriguing possibility is suggested by an apparent paradox: both mAChR-A and the dopamine receptor Damb signal through Gq (Himmelreich et al., 2017), but mAChR-A promotes learning while Damb promotes forgetting (Berry et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Himmelreich et al., 2017.

claim: Damb promotes forgetting.
source: Another intriguing possibility is suggested by an apparent paradox: both mAChR-A and the dopamine receptor Damb signal through Gq (Himmelreich et al., 2017), but mAChR-A promotes learning while Damb promotes forgetting (Berry et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Berry et al., 2012.

claim: Although damb mutants retain memories for longer than wildtype, their initial learning is slightly impaired.
source: Indeed, although damb mutants retain memories for longer than wildtype, their initial learning is slightly impaired (Berry et al., 2012); damb mutant larvae are also impaired in aversive olfactory learning (Selcho et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Berry et al., 2012.

claim: damb mutant larvae are impaired in aversive olfactory learning.
source: Indeed, although damb mutants retain memories for longer than wildtype, their initial learning is slightly impaired (Berry et al., 2012); damb mutant larvae are also impaired in aversive olfactory learning (Selcho et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Selcho et al., 2009.

claim: Gq signaling may aid both learning and forgetting by generally rendering synapses more labile.
source: Perhaps Gq signaling aids both learning and forgetting by generally rendering synapses more labile.
evidence: This is a speculation about the role of Gq signaling in synaptic plasticity.

claim: mAChR-A may allow a kind of metaplasticity in which exposure to odors makes flies' learning mechanisms more sensitive.
source: It is tempting to speculate that mAChR-A may allow a kind of metaplasticity (Abraham, 2008) in which exposure to odors (hence activation of mAChR-A in KCs) makes flies' learning mechanisms more sensitive.
evidence: This is a speculation about the potential role of mAChR-A in metaplasticity.

claim: Kenyon cells are subdivided into three main classes according to their innervation of the horizontal and vertical lobes of the MB: γ neurons, αβ neurons, and α′β′ neurons.
source: Kenyon cells are subdivided into three main classes according to their innervation of the horizontal and vertical lobes of the MB: γ neurons send axons only to the γ lobe of the horizontal lobes, while the axons of αβ and α′β′ neurons bifurcate and go to both the vertical and horizontal lobes (αβ axons make up the α lobe of the vertical lobe and β lobe of the horizontal lobe, while α′β′ axons make up the α′ lobe of the vertical lobe and β′ portion of the horizontal lobe).
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge about Kenyon cell subtypes.

claim: Different KC classes play different roles in olfactory learning.
source: These different classes play different roles in olfactory learning (Guven-Ozkan and Davis, 2014; Krashes et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Guven-Ozkan and Davis, 2014 and Krashes et al., 2007.

claim: γ, αβ and α′β′ KCs are thought to be important mainly for short-term memory, long-term memory, and memory consolidation, respectively.
source: Alternatively, γ, αβ and α′β′ KCs are thought to be important mainly for short-term memory, long-term memory, and memory consolidation, respectively (Guven-Ozkan and Davis, 2014; Krashes et al., 2007); as we only tested short-term memory, mAChR-A may carry out the same function in all KCs, but only its role in γ KCs is required for short-term (as opposed to long-term) memory.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Guven-Ozkan and Davis, 2014 and Krashes et al., 2007.

claim: The key plasticity gene DopR1 is required in γ, not αβ or α′β′ KCs, for short-term memory.
source: Indeed, the key plasticity gene DopR1 is required in γ, not αβ or α′β′ KCs, for short-term memory (Qin et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Qin et al., 2012.

claim: MB-MVP2 is an MBON postsynaptic to γ KCs required for aversive short-term memory.
source: Our finding that mAChR-A is required in γ KCs for aversive short-term memory is consistent with our finding that mAChR-A knockdown in KCs disrupts training-induced depression of odor responses in MB-MVP2, an MBON postsynaptic to γ KCs required for aversive short-term memory (Perisse et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Perisse et al., 2016.
